heading: Hook and context · 0:00–0:40
text: Ever wondered why your skin does not simply keep getting thicker, when cells in it go on dividing for your whole life? In a healthy adult tissue that is maintaining its size, cells are continually lost, worn away at the surface, and new cells made by mitosis replace them. Cells made and cells lost stay roughly in balance. Now picture one cell that stops keeping to that balance and just goes on dividing. That is where a tumour can begin.

heading: What you will be able to do · 0:40–1:05
text: By the end you will be able to explain how a mutation in a gene that controls cell division can lead to uncontrolled mitosis and a tumour; to tell a benign tumour from a malignant one; and to write that causal chain the way a mark scheme credits it.

heading: Division held in balance · 1:05–1:48
text: Look closer at the healthy tissue. Near the base, cells divide by mitosis; their daughter cells move up, become specialised and are eventually lost from the surface. Whether a cell divides again is not left to chance. Genes in the cell control when it goes round the cell cycle, so when cells are lost, division replaces them, and when the tissue is at its size, division is held back. A growing tissue, like a child's, makes more cells than it loses; this adult tissue stays level.

heading: A change in a control gene · 1:48–2:31
text: So what breaks the balance? The control depends on genes, and genes are lengths of DNA. A mutation is a change in the DNA sequence. One typical cause is ultraviolet radiation in sunlight: it reaches the cells of your skin and can cause mutations in them. Many such changes land nowhere near a gene that controls division. A change in a division-control gene can disrupt its function. Suppose that happens here: this cell loses control of its cell cycle and divides repeatedly when it should not.

heading: From one cell to a mass · 2:31–3:17
text: Here is why one faulty cell becomes a lump. Before it divides, the cell copies its DNA, mutated gene included, so both daughter cells inherit the mutation and also divide without control, and so do theirs. Picture a tap stuck open while the drain stays the same. Written properly: a mutation in a gene that controls cell division can cause loss of control, so the cell divides repeatedly by mitosis, producing a mass of abnormal cells, a tumour. Usually more than one such mutation has built up in the same cell line first.

heading: Benign or malignant · 3:17–3:51
text: A tumour is not always a cancer. A benign tumour typically stays in one place: it grows, usually within a clear boundary, and does not invade the tissue around it. A malignant tumour is a cancer. Its cells invade the surrounding tissue, and some can break away, travel in the blood or the lymph, and settle somewhere else. There they keep dividing without control and form secondary tumours.

heading: EXAM CONTRAST E5-07: mitosis named, control missing · 3:51–5:05
text: Here is an answer that would lose the mark. Our framing: a gene controlling cell division has mutated; explain how a tumour can form. Read this answer. Look at the word mitosis. It is tempting, since a tumour is built by cells dividing. Beyond the scheme, mitosis also repairs healthy tissue: naming it does not explain a tumour. What is missing is control. In this question the mutation is supplied; the marks are for its consequences. Loss of cell-cycle control allows repeated uncontrolled division, which builds a mass of abnormal cells. The scheme awards two marks for any two credited consequences. It does not require an extra named gene, a checkpoint protein or how the mutation arose. So, in place: the mutation causes loss of control of the cell cycle, so the cell divides repeatedly by mitosis without control, producing a mass of abnormal cells, a tumour.

heading: What I told you, on the tissue · 5:05–5:39
text: So here it is, on the tissue you watched. In balance, division replaces lost cells. A mutation in a gene controlling division, perhaps from ultraviolet light, can disrupt that control, as in our example. Daughter cells inherit it and divide repeatedly, building a mass: a tumour. A benign tumour typically stays put; a malignant one invades, and its cells can spread in blood or lymph to form secondary tumours.

heading: How it is asked, and the reject card · 5:39–6:12
text: How does this reach you? One written paper supplied the mutation and gave two marks for its consequences. Another supplied information about inhibitors and asked why they could treat a tumour, again for two marks: work from what it gives you. The reject card: a tumour is not automatically a cancer. Beyond the scheme, healthy adult skin maintains its size when cell production balances cell loss.
